name: Kaiwhekea
summary: Kaiwhekea is an extinct genus of plesiosaur from the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian age) of what is now New Zealand. Kaiwhekea belongs to the clade Aristonectinae inside the family Elasmosauridae.
credits: Author: QueenBella, with contributions from Lukesasa.
quickView: Kaiwhekea are Medium Cathemeral Aquatic Carnivores.
Kaiwhekea can group up to 8 sub/adults, up to 6 females and 2 males, unlimited offspring, unlimited adoptees.
Kaiwheka can have up to 3 Sub/Adults in an engagement or hunting party.
Kaiwhekea may hunt up to Large tier, but will prioritise unattended Leedsichthys offspring first, and then Medium tier above others, when in the area. Kaiwhekea may not scavenge.
Kaiwhekea flee from adult Spinosaurus and Deinosuchus.
Profile to be updated and extended soon!

blocks.text: Medium Cathemeral Aquatic Carnivore Kaiwhekea form promiscuous bonds. Kaiwhekea are nomadic. Kaiwhekea have a tolerant nature. Kaiwhekea may not scavenge from claimed corpses and must contest for a body. Critters and abandoned corpses may be freely eaten. Kaiwhekea tolerate albino and melanistic individuals.
Up to 8 Sub/Adults, consisting of 6 females and 2 males. Unlimited Offspring Unlimited Adoptees This group is known as a bale.

Skins that are considered mutations for Kaiwhekea include: Albino, Melanistic Players must roll in 🎲・genetics-rolls  to use these skins in game. This is one roll per species, per character. Only when the character dies can you roll again if using the same character name.

Up to 3 Sub/Adults may enter an engagement or hunt. Kaiwhekea flee from adult Spinosaurus and Deinosuchus. Kaiwhekea may hunt up to Large tier. Male Kaiwhekea do not protect offspring. Preferred Prey Kaiwhekea may hunt up to Large tier. However, if unattended Leedsichthys offspring are available, they must hunt these first. Afterwards, Kaiwhekea must hunt suitable Medium tier options before targeting Large tiers. Kaiwhekea flee from adult Spinosaurus and Deinosuchus. Offspring of these species, of adolescent and below, may be hunted. Kaiwhekea are unable to eat the bodies of Metriacanthosaurus without suffering averse side effects. See 📜・server-guideOPTIONAL - Illnesses & Injuries for more information.

🌧️ Rainy Season: 4 🥚 per 4 hours. ☀️ Dry Season: 2 🥚 per 4 hour. Kaiwhekea nest anywhere along the coastline or in shallow pools on coastal islands in their preferred POIs. Their nests are constructed out of kelp, branches and rocks. Kaiwhekea females may form same sex pairs.

♀️ Females are slimmer than males, and have duller colors. Suitable Subspecies include: tenui ♂️ Males are bulkier, with contrasting coloration. Suitable Subspecies include: katiki, grandis Physical dimorphism for Kaiwhekea is not mandatory, but individuals differing from the typical dimorphism may face difficulties during courtship.

Kaiwhekea hatchlings, known as calves, hatch fully developed and ready to swim after their mother - but do not do so until they reach Juvenile. Calves are born in shallow water - either along the coastline, or in shallow pools on coastal islands. From birth they watch their mother leave the tide pools to rejoin with her bale in deeper water, and wait behind in the shallows for safety. After reaching juvenile, they make the stretch across into deeper water to meet their maternal bale. Calves are precocial, ready to survive on their own and hunt small fish. However, calves do not begin hunting until sub-adult, and solely live on fish or shared kills from their bale until then. Despite this, calves do not rely on their mothers for food, and chase around fish and provide for themselves wherever possible. No calf will turn down the opportunity to share in their mother's kill, though! Calves enjoy play fighting with other calves within the bale.

Calves are able to survive on their own from the moment they hatch. Orphans without visible adults in the area become skittish, hiding in shallow water, the water surface, or around rocks away - from deep water predators. They take longer to emerge into deeper water than their counterparts with parents. Orphans may grow up to be more antisocial than most in their species.

Kaiwhekea are known as fast and agile swimmers, they swim near the surface, and enjoy leaping out of the water as a form of play with other Kaiwhekea. They can be spotted basking in shallow waters or even on land for a short period of time. With their long neck, small head, and sharp interlocking teeth, Kaiwhekea hunt small, soft-bodied prey such as fish or turtles. They use their keen eyesight to spot prey and avoid larger predators that share the ocean, unless desperate. Kaiwhekea are known to digest pebbles and shells to help digest the food they eat. Kaiwhekea take a great interest in terrestrial species they encounter near the water. Some attempt to get their attention by fetching them objects from the bottom of the seafloor to present as interesting trinkets.

Female Kaiwhekea are passive to their own kind, often forming loose groups up to 6 adults. They enjoy leaping out of the water with each other, and practising organised hunts, sometimes on one another. Though social, Kaiwhekea also enjoy their time alone, often sunbathing on beaches or swimming spread out from each other, careful not to get too close into one another's space. Male Kaiwhekea are less tolerant of each other, viewing the other as competition, but can occasionally form friendships and small duos with other males. These duos work together to drive away rival males during courtship and protect females. Female Kaiwhekea that spend a lot of time together in a bale sometimes end up forming same sex pairs. Though closely bonded with each other, they may still accept courtship advances from males, and raise offspring together with their female partner. Male Kaiwhekea do not stay with bales long-term, and slip away to find other females once their offspring reach adolescence.

Kaiwhekea are tolerant to their own species, and try to avoid conflict where possible - except during courtship. Ignoring is always the first option they consider when encountering aggression from other Kaiwhekea, and males that accidentally encroach too close to another male's females will quickly slip away, aware of the offence they may cause. Most Kaiwhekea greet each other warmly during migrations. If a male wishes to fight another male for his females, they bite and smack against each other in the water, fighting until one male backs down.

Kaiwhekea are tolerant to other species and try to avoid conflicts at all times. When finding new species they approach them with curiosity, often leading to being attacked if they turn out to be a predator. Kaiwhekea often swim to the bottom of the seafloor to retrieve an interesting item to present to a terrestrial species, enjoying the unusual interactions. Kaiwhekea always flee from adult Spinosaurus and Deinosuchus.

Kaiwhekea are opportunistic, intelligent and coordinated hunters. They can hunt up to Large tier, but will prioritise unattended Leedsichthys offspring first, and then Medium tier above others, when in the area. They flee from adult Spinosaurus and Deinosuchus. Kaiwhekea take it in turns swimming in to get bites on their prey.

During courting season, both sexes become extremely vocal underwater. These loud calls are used to locate a possible mate and also to evaluate and select the best mate for nesting. This loud vocalization can be divided into two categories: long-distance, and local calls. Long-distance calls, being like a broadcast, are used to find a mate over some distance. Repeated local calls, one after the other, are considered more friendly and submissive, and employed to signal interest in a mate. Males will court multiple females during one breeding season, if able to. If two different males happen to end up in the same area during courtship, they will usually try to drive the other one away. Males bellow loudly, trying to scare off the other male. When all fails, they bite and spin into each other until one reaches deathscars. These fights rarely end up in a dead male, but deep scars and bite marks are left on both. Even if male Kaiwhekea are in bonded duos, these males still fight to maintain breeding rights with the females. Offspring Rearing When preparing to nest, females will head to a coastal area with shallow pools, constructing a simple structure to lay their eggs. After all young hatch, mothers leave the shallow ponds and head out into deeper water to wait for their young to grow strong enough to join them. Once young have made the stretch into deeper water at juvenile, they travel around the oceans nomadically, with males swimming on the outside of the bale. Male Kaiwhekea do not participate in taking care of the offspring, but protect their selected bale until offspring are adolescent. Once young has reached adolescent, males return to a solitary or duo lifestyle.

When Kaiwhekea reach old age, they depart from their bale and seek deeper, hidden areas of the ocean. They will become less vocal and sometimes even shed into darker or duller coloration. Females that have formed a same sex bond can be found leaving a bale together. Elderly Kaiwhekea become weak near the end of their lifespan, with most dying due to lack of strength to bring them to resurface.
Kaiwhekea flee from adult Spinosaurus and Deinosuchus.
Kaiwhekea are unable to eat the bodies of Metriacanthosaurus without suffering averse side effects. See 📜・server-guideOPTIONAL - Illnesses & Injuries for more information. 4.4

solo.note: Solo gut machbar: Kaiwhekea verbringen laut Profil gern Zeit allein, sonnen sich und schwimmen verstreut. Männchen ziehen sowieso weiter, sobald ihre Jungen Adolescent sind. Die Jagdgrenze bis Large hängt nicht an der Gruppengröße.

playstyle.summary: Du bist ein Seelöwe mit der Gestalt einer Meeresschildkröte: ein schneller, verspielter Schwimmer mit langem Hals, der dicht unter der Oberfläche jagt, aus Spaß aus dem Wasser springt, kurz am Strand oder im Flachen döst und Landtieren neugierig Fundstücke vom Meeresgrund bringt. Du bist anderen Arten gegenüber friedlich, gehst Streit aus dem Weg und fliehst vor erwachsenen Spinosaurus und Deinosuchus. Wie eine Schildkröte bist du aber auch eine beliebte Beute schnellerer Meeresjäger, allen voran Eurhinosaurus. Solo bist du der Nomade der Küsten, der von Bucht zu Bucht zieht.

parts.title: Alltag: Schwimmen, Sonnen, Neugier
parts.text: Du bist Nomade im Salzwasser und ziehst entlang der Küsten: Kelp Vale im Norden, die Coastal Bluffs und die Volcano Islands, die Palm Islands, Stonebed Shoal und East Passage im Osten, und bei Bedarf die Abyssal Depths. Dazu kommen Brackwasser wie Coastland Swamp und die Mudflats. Du schwimmst dicht an der Oberfläche, springst zum Spaß, legst dich zum Sonnen ins flache Wasser oder für kurze Zeit an den Strand. Kiesel und Muscheln schluckst du für die Verdauung. Siehst du ein Landtier am Ufer, tauchst du nach einem hübschen Stück vom Meeresgrund und bringst es ihm. Das ist deine Art, Kontakt zu suchen, auch wenn es bei Räubern manchmal böse endet. Anderen Kaiwhekea begegnest du freundlich. Als Männchen hältst du Abstand zu fremden Weibchen, um keinen Kampf zu provozieren.

parts.title: Jagd
parts.text: Du darfst bis Large jagen, musst aber eine feste Reihenfolge einhalten: zuerst unbewachte Leedsichthys-Junge, dann passende Medium-Beute, erst danach Large. Jungtiere von Spinosaurus und Deinosuchus bis Adolescent darfst du jagen, deren Erwachsenen weichst du immer aus. Du bist ein wendiger Gelegenheitsjäger mit scharfen, verzahnten Zähnen. Im Wechsel stößt du hinein, beißt zu und drehst wieder ab. Deine Alltagsbeute sind Fische und weiche Tiere. Aas an beanspruchten Kadavern musst du streitig machen, Kleintiere und verlassene Kadaver sind frei. Metriacanthosaurus-Kadaver meidest du.

parts.title: Partnersuche & Balz
parts.text: Die Balz läuft wie im Profil. In der Balzzeit werdet ihr unter Wasser sehr laut: Mit fernen Rufen sucht ihr, mit kurzen, freundlichen Rufen zeigt ihr Interesse. Männchen umwerben mehrere Weibchen und kämpfen gegen Rivalen mit Bissen und Drehungen, meist bis Todesnarben, selten bis zum Tod. Genistet wird im flachen Wasser an der Küste oder in Tümpeln auf Küsteninseln, das Nest ist aus Kelp, Ästen und Steinen. Als Männchen ziehst du weiter, sobald die Jungen Adolescent sind. Das passt gut zum Solo-Leben.

opportunities.summary: Sarcosuchus is within the legal hunt ceiling. Kaiwhekea is 13% faster in water; a clean escape is unlikely once spotted. 1 Kaiwhekea vs 3 Sarcosuchus: the Sarcosuchus side wins in about 3 s with 93% of its health left.

intent.reason: Its profile permits hunting through Large tier.

chase.label: Kaiwhekea is 13% faster in water; a clean escape is unlikely once spotted.

encounter.label: They overlap in 3 mapped areas, so the matchup is situational.

facts: Its profile permits hunting through Large tier.

1 Kaiwhekea vs 3 Sarcosuchus: the Sarcosuchus side wins in about 3 s with 93% of its health left.
They overlap in 3 mapped areas, so the matchup is situational.

methodology.intent: Profile-specific hunt, prey, rivalry and avoidance rules are checked before tier eligibility.
methodology.pursuit: Relevant land, water or flight caps and sprint duration determine whether contact can be forced.
methodology.groups: By default you are solo and the other side brings its full legal group; both sides can be set to any size up to the profile caps. Unlimited groups are never turned into an invented number.
methodology.fight: Every hit is resolved as damage × (attacker CW ÷ victim CW) ÷ victim armour from the adult stat curves. Each side focus-fires one target at a time with its best spammable attack plus up to two stronger abilities. Times assume every swing lands, so agile, smaller players outperform them by dodging. Bleed stacks, ignores armour and blocks healing; it is shown as pressure and only converted into health when you switch on the estimate, because that rate is not documented.
methodology.encounter: Mapped area overlap lowers or raises relevance, but an explicit cross-species rule can override sparse map overlap.

analog.label: Sea lion + Sea turtle
analog.headline: A sea-lion colony in a long-necked, turtle-like body: basks on beaches, plays in the surf, hunts in turns.
analog.playsLike: You are a medium aquatic carnivore in a 'bale' of up to 6 females and 2 males. You are curious and friendly, fetching trinkets from the seafloor for land animals, but also a capable coordinated hunter: up to 3 take turns biting prey up to Large tier, starting with unattended Leedsichthys young and then Medium tier. You flee adult Spinosaurus and Deinosuchus, and Tylosaurus hunts you before anything else.

setting.label: Open sea, coasts and beaches
setting.note: Nomadic aquatic. Swims near the surface and basks in shallows or briefly on land.

analogs.covers: Life: colony of females with a couple of males, beach basking, playful leaping, curious about land animals

credit.artist: (c) Jonathan Eisen, some rights reserved (CC BY)

analogs.covers: Body and role: a gentle, long-necked glider that basks and ends up as the favourite prey of faster sea hunters

why.text: Up to 6 females and 2 males. Male duos drive off rival males and males fight each other for females. Sea lion colonies look the same.
Leaps out of the water in play and basks in shallow water or on land.
Approaches new species with curiosity and fetches objects from the seafloor to present to land animals.
Opportunistic, intelligent, coordinated: members take turns swimming in to bite.
Tylosaurus must hunt Kaiwhekea first and Eurhinosaurus torments it. Orcas hunt sea lions and turtles the same way. A group of turtles is also called a 'bale' (official inspiration: sea turtles).

notLike: Sea turtles don't hunt big prey; Kaiwhekea takes up to Large tier.
Sea lions haul out on land for long stretches; Kaiwhekea only basks on land for a short time.

modes.note: Kaiwhekea verbringen laut Profil gern Zeit allein, sonnen sich und schwimmen verstreut, wie Seelöwen am Strand. Die Jagdgrenze hängt nicht an der Gruppe.
